title: RBI increases repo rate to 5 . 50 %: How does it impact a consumer ?
text:
A Correspondent
GUWAHATI: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday announced an increase in the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% from 5.25% to tackle rising inflation, which moved beyond the 4% target. The increase marks the first repo rate hike by the central bank in nearly four years.
With the increase, consumers and borrowers will need to shell out more for goods/services and in loan EMIs, respectively. Let us understand the economics behind the repo rate and how it impacts the banks, markets, and consumers, especially the salaried middle class.
What is repo rate?
In simple terms, the repo rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks. An increase in the repo rate means that the borrowing banks have to pay more to the RBI during repayment.
How does it impact the consumer?
Once the repo rate is increased, the borrowing banks pass most of the added burden to the consumers by either hiking the loan interest rates or increasing the payment tenure. In both cases, the borrower will pay more.
The salaried middle class is the worst-hit, as most of the essential goods and commodities, like houses, vehicles, and other urgent requirements, are often met by this category with home loans, vehicle loans, and personal loans.
As an example, with the current increase in the repo rate by 25 basis points, a person who would have paid a total interest of Rs 54,13,840 on a loan of Rs 50,00,000 at the rate of 8.50% for a tenure of 20 years will now have to pay a total interest of Rs 56,04,400, which is an increase of Rs 1,90,560.
Why is repo rate increased or decreased?
The RBI, as the central bank of the country, changes the repo rate to keep the inflation rate in check. When the inflation rate is higher, the RBI aims to 'bring back the money' in the market and decrease the demand for goods/services.
Once interest rates on loans are increased, consumers postpone their purchase plans for later, which decreases the demand for the product and subsequently reduces their price, thus keeping inflation in check.
Apart from rising inflation, the current repo hike was fuelled by spiking crude oil prices amid unrest in the Middle East and a weaker rupee. However, the strong GDP growth projections for FY27 at 7.1% allowed the RBI some flexibility while increasing the repo rate.

title: Why have SLBCs / UTLBCs been asked to report SC beneficiary data for key government schemes for jobs and entrepreneurship ?: Explained
text:
The story so far:
The Finance Ministry has now directed State-level and UT-level Bankers’ Committees to mandatorily include data on the percentage share of SC beneficiaries availing flagship Central schemes such as the Mudra Yojana, Stand Up India, Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme, MSME/business loans, and others. This direction comes after a nudge from the National Commission for Scheduled Castes flagged the fact that these bankers’ committees were not reporting this data for a number of these government schemes in their regular reviews, which was hindering the Commission’s ability to perform its Constitutional duties.
What are SLBCs/UTLBCs?
According to the Reserve Bank of India, the State Level Bankers’ Committees are the “apex inter-institutional forum to facilitate coordination in the efforts of the State Government, banks, financial institutions and other relevant stakeholders, for the development of the State”. In Union Territories, this is known as the UTLBC (Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committees). These committees are usually chaired by a Convener Bank that is notified by the RBI.
The Committees comprise the heads of relevant State government departments, the RBI Regional Director, State heads of commercial banks with a major presence in the concerned State, NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development), Regional Rural Banks, and the State co-operative bank. Apart from these members, RBI guidelines require that the committees invite representatives of institutions like the National Commissions for SCs and STs, the National Horticulture Board, farmers’ unions, and other stakeholders. These committees are mandated to meet every quarter.
The primary focus of the SLBS is supposed to be on “policy and strategic issues relating to the flow of priority sector credit and overall financial inclusion in the state”, as per the RBI guidelines governing the functioning of the committees.
What did the National Commission for Scheduled Castes notice in recent meetings of SLBCs/UTLBCs?
The National Commission for SCs has a Constitutional mandate to participate and advise on matters related to planning the socio-economic development of SC communities across the country. One of the ways that the National Commission performs this function is by attending meetings of SLBCs/UTLBCs, in addition to conducting regular reviews of public institutions that SC communities interact with.
According to a letter written to the Union Finance Ministry’s Department of Financial Services, the National Commission for Scheduled Castes noted that one hurdle in performing its review function at SLBCs and UTLBCs was the absence of data on the share of SC beneficiaries for several Union government schemes that are meant to provide subsidised business loans, generate employment, and formalise street vending business in the country, among others.
NCSC Secretary, Vivek K. Dewangan, said in his September 24 letter to the DFS that the SLBC convener banks were not reflecting this data, based on observations made by State representatives of the Commission who have been attending the meetings of these bankers’ committees across States and UTs. The NCSC asked the DFS to issue necessary directions to the committees to report this data mandatorily and for this data to be relayed to the Commission.
The schemes flagged by the NCSC for specific scheme-wise and bank-wise data on SC beneficiaries included the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana, Stand-Up India entrepreneurship loan scheme, Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme, PM SVANidhi (PM Street Vendors’ Atma Nirbhar Nidhi), Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises, and MSME Business Loans, among others.
Why does the NCSC need data on SC beneficiaries for these schemes?
Government officials explained that a major function of the Commission at the SLBC and UTLBC review meetings is to evaluate the level of financial inclusion of SC families. This requires them to gather data on the number and share of SC beneficiaries across schemes and banks, they said. “The purpose is to determine whether the share of SC beneficiaries for each scheme roughly matches the share of these communities in the respective population of the States or UTs,” one official said, elaborating further, “For example, if a State has roughly 10% SC population, we would expect that the share of SC beneficiaries in schemes would be as close to this as practically possible.”
What have the SLBCs/UTLBCs been told to do to address this issue?
In response to the issue flagged by the NCSC, the Department of Financial Services has written an advisory to all SLBCs/UTLBCs on October 5, asking them to ensure that data on both the number and share of SC beneficiaries - both scheme-wise and bank-wise is included in the review reports. The DFS has noted that this data should also be shared with the NCSC regularly, further giving the committees time till October 9 to raise any issue they may have with the availability of such data on SC beneficiaries.

title: Ambani Jio said to seek about Rs 11 lakh crore valuation in IPO
text:
The telecom and digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries Ltd. has finished gauging demand for the offering and is likely to begin meetings with potential investors this week to discuss valuation and pricing, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.
India’s largest wireless operator is looking to open its IPO the week of Oct. 19 and list before Oct. 30, the people said. Deliberations are ongoing and the final dates, valuation and other details could change, they said.
A representative for Jio didn’t immediately respond to a request for comments.
The valuation would also make Jio India’s third most valuable publicly traded company, behind parent Reliance, which has a market capitalization of about $169 billion. Bharti Airtel Ltd., Jio’s main telecommunications rival, is valued at about $116 billion.
National Stock Exchange of India Ltd., which was forced to downsize its deal. In June, local brokerage Motilal Oswal Financial Services estimated Jio’s valuation at between $115 billion and $118 billion, while Dolat Capital valued the company at around $110 billion.
Jio’s offering adds to an already busy year for India’s IPO market. Listing proceeds surpassed $9 billion in the July-September quarter, the most ever for the period, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That pushed fundraising so far this year to more than $13 billion.
The company has appointed 19 banks to work on the share sale, including Kotak Mahindra Capital Co., Morgan Stanley, BofA Securities Inc., Axis Capital Ltd., BNP Paribas and Citigroup Inc.

title: NCLT panel says Jaypee Infratech failed to deliver projects within the promised timelines
text:
A fact-finding committee appointed by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has concluded that Jaypee Infratech Ltd (JIL), taken over by a consortium led by Suraksha Realty Limited under an approved resolution plan, failed to complete projects within the promised timelines, leaving thousands of homebuyers waiting for possession.
The two-member committee, comprising former NCLT Members Prasanta Kumar Mohanty and Dr Deepti Mukesh, submitted its final report on August 20, covering the progress of all 19 JIL projects as of June 30, 2026.
It found that homebuyers’ grievances over construction delays and non-delivery were “correct and genuine” and urged the NCLT to take “urgent cognizance” of the lapses and issue appropriate compliance directions.
The NCLT had approved the resolution plan submitted by Suraksha Realty Limited and Lakshdeep Investments and Finance Private Limited in March 2023, a decision upheld by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) in May 2024. The consortium subsequently took charge of JIL.
Of JIL’s 250 residential towers, 91 comprising 12,867 units had been completed before the successful resolution applicant (SRA) took charge. The remaining 159 towers comprise 97 stalled towers with 10,164 units and 62 near-complete towers involving 6,067 units.
The SRA was required to complete the residual work on the 62 near-complete towers within 18 months, including the six-month period and one-year grace period. However, over two years, it issued 3,444 offers of possession and executed 2,614 sub-lease deeds. The committee said more than 6,000 offers could have been issued if the obligation had been met.
Progress on the 97 stalled towers, meanwhile, could not be independently verified, with the committee saying the SRA’s data lacked credibility.
Labour shortfall
The committee identified inadequate labour deployment as one of the principal reasons for the delays. The resolution plan envisaged about 12,000 labourers, but the SRA reported an average deployment of 1,787 workers in January-March 2025, 4,735 in January-March 2026 and 5,415 in April-June 2026.
During site visits, however, the committee observed only 200-300 workers at some locations and estimated actual deployment at around 3,500-4,000. It rejected the SRA’s contention that more than 5,000 workers were neither required nor available, saying the position was “neither acceptable nor credible”. It recommended deploying 12,000 or more workers immediately.
The panel also found homebuyers’ concerns over the quality of steel being used to be genuine. It noted that steel other than that supplied by manufacturers such as SAIL and Tata was being used and stressed that quality could not be compromised in 30-32-storey towers located in an earthquake-prone area.
The report flagged several other breaches, including the failure to arrange a Rs 3,000 crore working-capital facility required under the resolution plan. It also found that three instalments totalling Rs 666 crore towards additional farmer compensation ordered by the NCLAT remained unpaid as of May 24, 2026.
The committee further noted that monthly progress reports mandated by the NCLT had not been filed since the SRA took over in June 2024. It described the Project Monitoring Committee as “ineffective” and said funds earmarked for construction had been diverted to associate entities and invested in mutual funds. An FIR registered in January alleges diversion of about Rs 300 crore; the SRA has said the transactions were subsequently reversed.
Suraksha exit questioned
The committee also questioned the departure of Suraksha Realty, one of the two resolution applicants. In an affidavit, the SRA said Suraksha had been “duly discharged” and had no role in implementation, leaving Lakshdeep Investments and Finance Private Limited to carry out the plan.
The committee said the circumstances of the exit lacked clarity and noted that the resolution plan made both applicants jointly and severally responsible. It found it “surprising” that one applicant could withdraw without informing stakeholders or seeking the tribunal’s clearance while the plan remained unimplemented. It also said it was unclear whether Suraksha was still associated with JIL when the alleged diversion of funds occurred.
Delays were also reported in villas, plots and commercial units. At Kingswood Oriental, seven of 37 villas remained incomplete, while only 18 possession offers had been issued for 652 commercial units across three projects.
The committee also backed plot allottees at Agra Kensington Park, where the SRA had scrapped development and offered refunds. After inspecting the 850-acre site, it found the land well located, without encroachment, and said the SRA should allot the plots “without loss of time.”
No fresh resolution plan
The committee identified interest, penal charges and transfer fees as another major grievance. It said no interest or penal interest should be charged for the insolvency moratorium period between August 9, 2017 and June 4, 2024, when banks did not disburse loans. It also recommended resolving transfer-charge issues, saying this could benefit more than 10,000 buyers.
Despite its findings, the committee advised against inviting fresh resolution plans, noting that construction and deliveries were continuing, although not strictly according to the approved timelines.
Instead, it recommended restructuring the monitoring mechanism. This includes reconstituting the Project Monitoring Committee within a month, appointing an Independent Observer to the JIL board, renewing the Rs 100 crore performance bank guarantee through February 2028 and allowing lenders to sell allotted land parcels transparently.
The SRA told the committee that there was no shortage of funds, citing Rs 1,403 crore in cash and equivalents as of March 31, 2026, along with expected hospital-sale proceeds of about Rs 600 crore and monthly toll collections of Rs 50-60 crore from the Yamuna Expressway. However, the committee found the claim of adequate funds unconvincing in view of the slow construction, labour shortfall and unpaid YEIDA instalments.
The decision on penalising the SRA or taking any stronger action now rests with the NCLT.

title: Before Sabarmati , Kochrab ashram was Gandhi first laboratory for social change
text:
Speaking about its historical significance, Gandhi's great-grandson Tushar Gandhi noted that Bapu's decision to house a Dalit family at Kochrab sparked local backlash, ultimately compelling him to relocate across the city to set up Sabarmati Ashram in 1917.
While Sabarmati Ashram remains a must-visit site for tourists and dignitaries alike, the "Satyagrah Ashram" at Kochrab in Ahmedabad, founded by Gandhi in May 1915, became the first base for him to put into practice principles of truth, non-violence, simplicity and discipline, and champion the cause of social equality and self-reliance.

"It was here that Gandhiji invited a Dalit family to reside, a move that sparked rebellion among many of his associates and led to his social ostracism, eventually compelling him to move to Sabarmati Ashram in June 1917, a little over two years later," said Tushar Gandhi, a noted author and human rights activist.
Gandhian thought at the Central University of Gujarat.
"From this ashram, Gandhi put the principles of truth, non-violence, simplicity, and discipline into practice, while voicing opposition to untouchability, and championing the cause of social equality and self-reliance, 'Swadeshi' (indigenous self-reliance) and self-sufficiency through the use of the 'takli' (hand spindle) and the 'charkha' (spinning wheel)," he said.
A colonial-style building with a white-washed facade, Kochrab Ashram also became the ground for his opposition to untouchability and advocacy for social equality and self-reliance, he said.
The Kochrab Ashram now houses a Gandhi Memorial Museum with a collection of artefacts associated with his life and historical photographs. It has a large portrait of Gandhiji and his wife Kasturba, along with those of Leo Tolstoy, John Ruskin and Shrimad Rajchandra, and some of the historical artefacts on display here are Gandhiji's iconic wooden writing desk and a wooden spinning wheel, 'charkha.'
Upon his return from South Africa, Gandhiji moved into the ashram at Paldi, Ahmedabad in May 1915. He renamed the structure, which stood in stark contrast to everything in the city, as 'Satyagraha Ashram'.
Two years later, he shifted to a piece of open land on the banks of the Sabarmati River and engaged in constructive activities, including cattle breeding, spinning khadi, and such, and became one of the main centres for the Indian freedom struggle. He stayed here till 1930.
